sql_schemas: table notifications | fields: id, recipient_id, type, title, message, related_entity_type, related_entity_id, related_entity_code, status, created_at, read_at | pk: id | fks: recipient_id -> employees.id | indexes: id: primary key; the findById lookup and the updateStatus target.; recipient_id, status: the approver's inbox read pattern — the consumer of this feature's notification — and the existing composite index from the initial migration.; related_entity_type, related_entity_id: correlates a notification with the leave request it concerns; the approver notice carries the request id here. Specified in the GP-008 section but ABSENT from the initial migration — reconcile before adding.; related_entity_code: deliberately NOT indexed — it is only ever read as part of a row already located by id or by recipient, so no query this feature issues would use it.

table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at, reverses_request_id | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id; reverses_request_id -> leave_requests.id | indexes: id: primary key; the findById lookup that every cancel and every single-read starts from.; employee_id, status: the composite index the initial migration already creates; serves the role-scoped list queries and the owner/status guards. It does NOT serve the pending-decisions query, which filters on status and approver_id with no employee_id predicate.; status: the pending-decisions filter. The existing index is (employee_id, status), so a status-only predicate cannot use it as a leading column — this feature's queue query is the first status-only access path in the codebase and is the reason a standalone status index is required.; approver_id: the pending-decisions predicate for an APPROVED request (approver_id = actor.id) and the recipient resolution for a cancelled APPROVED request. Not indexed today; approver_id is an FK with no supporting index.; leave_type_code, start_date: type filter, inclusive date-range filter, and ORDER BY start_date DESC.; reverses_request_id (UNIQUE, nullable): the GP-008 linkage and the DB backstop for exactly-once balance release. A cancelled-after-approval request is TWO rows — the original APPROVED row and the CANCELLED reversal — so any pending-decisions query MUST exclude rows whose reverses_request_id is non-null, or the reversal row is a second, spurious queue entry.; employee_id: FK lookups and per-employee history.

table employees | fields: id, employee_number, first_name, last_name, email, password_hash, role, manager_id, department, hire_date, termination_date, employment_status | pk: id | fks: manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: id: primary key; the FK target for leave_requests.employee_id / approver_id / cancelled_by and notifications.recipient_id.; manager_id: the direct-report lookup. This feature reads it in the opposite direction — resolving a requester's direct manager for a SUBMITTED cancellation — via the existing getEmployeeById(requesterId).managerId, so the index is not strictly required for that read; it remains load-bearing for getEmployeesByManagerId and for the role-scoped visibility rule.; email (unique): login lookup; unchanged by this feature.; employee_number (unique): natural key; unchanged by this feature.

methods: create(input: CreateLeaveRequestInput, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest> — EXISTING, unchanged. Inserts all 15 columns including reverses_request_id; used for the GP-008 CANCELLED reversal row.
findById(id: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest | null> — EXISTING, unchanged. Returns null when absent; the service decides error semantics.
findByReversesRequestId(reversesRequestId: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest | null> — EXISTING, unchanged. The double-cancel guard for an APPROVED request.

update(id: string, changes: UpdateLeaveRequestDto, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest> — EXISTING, unchanged. Dynamic SET from FIELD_COLUMNS; used ONLY for the in-place DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancellation. MUST NOT be called with the id of an APPROVED row (GP-008).

findByQuery(params: LeaveRequestQueryParams, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest[]> — EXISTING, unchanged. Status/leaveTypeCode/date-range/employeeIds filters plus limit/offset, ORDER BY start_date DESC.

findPendingDecisions(approverId: string, client?: PoolClient): Promise<LeaveRequest[]> — NEW. Returns the requests still awaiting this approver's decision: status = SUBMITTED AND employee_id <> approverId (the queue the approver would decide), UNION the requests this approver already decided and that remain APPROVED — status = APPROVED AND approver_id = approverId. Excludes every row with reverses_request_id IS NOT NULL (a GP-008 reversal row is terminal and inert and must never appear as a decision). Excludes status = CANCELLED by construction, which is what makes a cancelled request stop being listed. ORDER BY start_date ASC, id ASC (oldest decision first, deterministic tie-break). Returns an array, possibly empty — never null, never throws on no rows. Read-only: takes no forUpdate, opens no transaction.

data_notes:
PERSISTENCE SLICE — Notify the approver when a leave request is cancelled.

TABLES. Three tables are touched; two are unchanged and one gains a column. No new table is introduced.
- `notifications` (EXTENDED): gains `related_entity_code` (nullable) so the approver's cancellation notice can carry the leave type alongside the request id, satisfying "the approver can act without a second lookup". Without it the leave type is only reachable by joining back to `leave_requests` — the second lookup the requirement forbids. `related_entity_id` carries the request id; `related_entity_type` stays the existing `'leave_request'` discriminator. The column is generic (a code for whatever `related_entity_type` names), not leave-specific, so the single notifications table stays the one notification concept.
- `leave_requests` (UNCHANGED, referenced by name): already carries `status`, `approver_id`, `cancelled_at`, `cancelled_by` and `reverses_request_id`. No column is added. It is the source for both the recipient resolution (APPROVED → `approver_id`; SUBMITTED → the requester's `employees.manager_id`) and the pending-decisions query.
- `employees` (UNCHANGED, referenced by name): `manager_id` resolves the SUBMITTED recipient.
- `audit_logs` and `leave_balances` are unchanged and are listed only as participants in the cancellation unit of work.

INDEXES. Two are genuinely new and both are load-bearing for this feature:
- `leave_requests.status` standalone. The existing index is `(employee_id, status)`, so a status-only predicate cannot use it as a leading column. The pending-decisions query filters on status with no employee_id predicate — it is the first status-only access path in the codebase.
- `leave_requests.approver_id`. The pending-decisions predicate for an APPROVED request, and the recipient resolution for a cancelled APPROVED request. `approver_id` is an FK with no supporting index today.
The pending-decisions query MUST also exclude rows with `reverses_request_id IS NOT NULL`: a cancelled-after-approval request is TWO rows (the original APPROVED row plus the CANCELLED reversal), so without that predicate the reversal row is a spurious second queue entry. The UNIQUE index on `reverses_request_id` already exists and is the DB backstop for exactly-once balance release.

REPOSITORIES. One new method, on an existing interface: `ILeaveRepository.findPendingDecisions(approverId, client?)` → `PgLeaveRequestRepository` (PostgreSQL via the shared pg Pool). `INotificationRepository`/`PgNotificationRepository` is extended end-to-end for `related_entity_code` (COLUMNS, NotificationRow, mapRow, INSERT). `IAuditRepository`, `IBalanceRepository` and `IEmployeeRepository` are unchanged; their contracts are recorded because they participate in the cancellation unit of work or in recipient resolution. Every method keeps the optional trailing `PoolClient` defaulting to the shared pool; no repository opens BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK.

CONCERNS SURFACED (not silently resolved).
1. The scope says a SUBMITTED cancellation notifies "the requester's direct manager", but `employees.manager_id` is nullable and the seeded employee has `manager_id = null`. The recipient is genuinely unresolvable for a reachable case, and the scope does not say whether the cancellation then fails or notifies nobody. Recorded as an open question rather than asserted.
2. The scope requires the notification to carry the leave type, but the notifications table has no column for it. The `related_entity_code` addition is the option this spec assumes; the alternatives are recorded as an open question because it is a once-per-table schema decision.
3. Documented-vs-built drift: the GP-008 section of docs/ARCHITECTURE.md specifies a `(related_entity_type, related_entity_id)` index on notifications, but the initial migration creates only `(recipient_id, status)`. This feature is the first to write a notification whose entity linkage is load-bearing, so the drift becomes reachable here. Flagged, not silently fixed.
4. The scope says nothing about the existing requester notification that `cancel` already sends, so the notification count per cancellation is undecided.
5. `GET /leaves/pending-decisions` does not exist in any form (no route, no service method, no repository query), and the scope states only that it must stop listing a cancelled request. Its membership rule is undecided, and that rule determines the query's predicates and which indexes are needed.

CONSISTENCY WITH EXISTING ARCHITECTURE. This extends the GP-008 reversal semantics rather than contradicting them: the reversal row is terminal and inert, so it is excluded from the queue and never itself notified about. The audit entry for a cancellation is explicitly unchanged (one `AuditAction.CANCEL` record keyed to the ORIGINAL request id). The recipient resolution reuses the existing one-level-only manager rule and the existing `getEmployeeById` read rather than introducing a second visibility rule. No new module, no new table, no new dependency edge: `leave` already depends on `notification`, `audit`, `balance` and `employee`.

open_questions.question: When a SUBMITTED request is cancelled and the requester has no direct manager (employees.manager_id is null), who is notified — and does the cancellation still succeed?
open_questions.impact: The scope says a SUBMITTED cancellation notifies 'the requester's direct manager'. employees.manager_id is nullable and the seeded employee has manager_id = null, so the recipient is genuinely unresolvable for a real, reachable case. This decides whether the cancellation can fail, silently notify nobody, or notify a substitute — and it is the difference between a 200 and a 409 on POST /leaves/:id/cancel. It must be decided once for the whole feature, not per call site.
candidate_options: Notify nobody and record only the audit entry (the cancellation still succeeds)
Fall back to the requester's manager's manager (transitive escalation) — contradicts the one-level-only visibility rule
Fall back to any ADMIN (a role-wide broadcast, not a single approver)
Reject the cancellation with ConflictError when no approver can be resolved

open_questions.question: How is the leave type persisted on the approver's cancellation notification, given the notifications table has no column for it?
open_questions.impact: The scope requires the notification to carry the request id AND the leave type so the approver can act without a second lookup. The notifications table has related_entity_type/related_entity_id but no column for a second domain value, and the leave type is not derivable from the request id without a join back to leave_requests — which is exactly the second lookup the requirement forbids. This is a schema decision that must be made once for the table, not worked around per call site.
candidate_options: Add a nullable related_entity_code column to notifications (the option this spec assumes) — one migration, no new table
Add a nullable related_entity_id_secondary column — opaque, no domain meaning
Encode the leave type into the existing message text only — no schema change, but the approver cannot act without parsing prose
Introduce a dedicated leave_cancellation_notices table — a second notification concept, contradicting the single notifications table

open_questions.question: The notifications table's documented (related_entity_type, related_entity_id) index does not exist in the initial migration — add it now, or treat the documentation as the error?
open_questions.impact: The GP-008 section of docs/ARCHITECTURE.md specifies a (related_entity_type, related_entity_id) index on notifications, but migrations/20260913000000_initial_schema.js creates only (recipient_id, status). The documented conceptual schema and the built schema disagree. This feature is the first to write a notification whose entity linkage is load-bearing, so the drift becomes reachable here. It must be resolved once for the table rather than assumed by one query.
candidate_options: Add the (related_entity_type, related_entity_id) index in this feature's migration — the GP-008 spec already claims it exists
Add it as a separate, explicitly-scoped migration so the drift is visible
Leave it unindexed — the approver notice is read by recipient_id, not by entity, so no query this feature issues needs it
Audit the whole initial migration against the documented conceptual tables and reconcile every drift at once

open_questions.question: Does the approver notification replace, or coexist with, the existing requester notification that cancel already sends?
open_questions.impact: The scope says 'send one notification to the approver' and 'keep the existing audit entry unchanged', but says nothing about the existing requester notification that cancel already sends. If the canceller is the requester (the common case for DRAFT/SUBMITTED), the requester is notified about their own action. This decides the notification count per cancellation — a quantity that must hold across every cancellation path (DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED reversal) rather than being asserted per call site.
candidate_options: One notification per cancellation event, to the approver only — the requester's existing notice is unchanged (the option this spec assumes)
One notification per cancellation event, to the approver, and suppress the requester's notice when the canceller IS the requester (they already know)
One notification per cancellation event, to the approver, and keep the requester's notice unconditionally
One notification per recipient, deduplicated when approver and requester are the same person

open_questions.question: What is the exact membership rule for GET /leaves/pending-decisions — SUBMITTED only, or SUBMITTED plus the APPROVED requests this approver decided?
open_questions.impact: The scope states only that the endpoint 'must stop listing a request once it is cancelled'. It does not say what the endpoint lists today, and no such endpoint exists in the codebase (no route, no service method, no repository query). The membership rule determines the query's predicates, which indexes it needs, and whether approver_id must be indexed at all. It must be decided once for the endpoint, not inferred from one query.
candidate_options: SUBMITTED only — the queue is the set of requests awaiting a decision; an APPROVED request is already decided (the option this spec assumes)
SUBMITTED plus APPROVED — the approver keeps a record of what they decided, and a cancelled APPROVED request disappears from it
SUBMITTED plus APPROVED plus REJECTED — a full decision history
SUBMITTED only, and the endpoint is renamed to reflect that it is a queue rather than a decision history

transaction_contract:
REQUIRED — this feature has multi-step writes that must be atomic. Cancelling a SUBMITTED or APPROVED request performs, in ONE unit of work: (a) the status change — an in-place `update` to CANCELLED for SUBMITTED, or the GP-008 insert of a NEW CANCELLED reversal row for APPROVED; (b) the balance release — `pendingDays -= requestedDays` for SUBMITTED, `usedDays -= requestedDays` for APPROVED; (c) the CANCEL audit entry (unchanged in shape); (d) the approver notification insert. The scope makes (d) explicitly non-optional: "it must be sent inside the same unit of work as the status change, so a failure to notify cannot leave a cancelled request with no record of the notification attempt." A failed notification insert must therefore roll back the status change and the balance release.

PROPAGATION ACROSS THE CALLER-CONTROLLED BOUNDARY. Repository and service methods that must join a caller's transaction take an OPTIONAL trailing `client?: PoolClient` parameter, defaulting to the shared pool (`src/shared/db/connection.ts`) when omitted. The calling service owns the unit of work: `LeaveService.cancel` calls `this.uow.withTransaction(async (client) => { ... })`. `PgUnitOfWork` acquires a client from the shared pool, issues BEGIN, runs the callback, COMMITs on resolve / ROLLBACKs on throw, and always releases the client. Inside the callback the SAME `client` is threaded to every participating call: `repository.findByReversesRequestId(originalId, client)`, `repository.update(id, changes, client)` or `repository.create(reversalInput, client)`, `balanceRepository.findByKey(..., client, true)` (row lock) then `balanceRepository.update(balanceId, changes, client)`, `auditService.record(entry, client)`, and `notificationService.create(input, client)`. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK appear ONLY in `PgUnitOfWork` — never in a repository or a service.

RECIPIENT RESOLUTION INSIDE THE TRANSACTION. The approver is resolved before the notification insert and inside the same callback: for an APPROVED request, `request.approverId` (already on the row, no extra read); for a SUBMITTED request, `employeeService.getEmployeeById(request.employeeId).managerId`. The employee read is a read-only lookup and takes no client — it joins no transaction and must not be made to. A DRAFT cancellation notifies nobody and, matching the existing rule that a DRAFT cancellation touches no balance, performs no balance read or write; it still runs inside the same unit of work for its status change and audit entry.

READ PATHS. `GET /leaves/pending-decisions` is read-only: it opens NO transaction and forwards NO client. `findPendingDecisions` takes no `forUpdate` and no client. The existing `list`/`getById`/`getHistory` read paths are unchanged and likewise open no transaction.
